summary: Describes how the IETF picks its representative for the ICANN Root Zone Evolution Review Committee (RZERC). It is a process memo about an appointment, not a technical protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When a club needs to send one person to a big meeting, it needs a way to pick who goes. This is the club's rule for picking.

subtitle: How the IAB picks the IETF's delegate to ICANN's Root Zone Evolution Review Committee.

tldr.problem: The RZERC charter calls on the IETF to name a delegate to the committee, and the IETF needed a defined way to choose one.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB selects one person for a one-year term, renewable for up to three additional one-year terms, after a public call for nominations and a review of nominees.
tldr.outcome: The memo sets qualifications, a timeframe aimed at ICANN's annual general meeting in Q4, and an interim process for mid-term vacancies. It has no technical protocol content.

facts.label: Renewals
facts.value: Up to three additional one-year terms

today: RFC 8128 is an Informational RFC from March 2017, published by the IAB. The metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Role and the Process
sections.content:
The ICANN Root Zone Evolution Review Committee (RZERC) reviews proposed architectural changes to the content of the DNS root zone, the systems used to execute changes, and the mechanisms for distributing the root zone, and makes recommendations to the ICANN Board. Its charter calls on the IETF to name a delegate.

The IAB-run process described here has the IAB solicit public input and make the selection.
sections.plainLanguage: A big group about the internet's address book wants one person from the IETF. This memo says how that person is chosen.

sections.title: Desirable Qualifications
sections.content:
Candidates should have demonstrable IETF involvement, especially active participation in working groups, and clearly demonstrated technical competence in Internet technology relating to the DNS root zone. They should be able to explain technical issues so the ICANN Board gets sound perspectives, and understand the roles of the IETF and ICANN.

The candidate is a representative or delegate of the IETF and should be able to call on IETF experts as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The person should know the IETF well, understand the root of the DNS, and explain hard ideas clearly.

sections.title: Term, Nomination and Selection
sections.content:
The appointment is a one-year term, renewable for up to three additional one-year terms. If the incumbent is willing and within the limits, the IAB may ask the community for feedback and, if a full process is unnecessary, reappoint them for another year.

Otherwise the IAB makes a public call for nominations on the IETF Announce mailing list. Self-nominations are permitted and all IETF participants are eligible; IAB members who accept a nomination recuse themselves from selection discussions. The IAB publishes the list of nominees, reviews the material, makes a selection and considers conflicts with other ICANN committees.

The aim is to seat new members in time for ICANN's annual general meeting in Q4, with 4-6 weeks for nominations or incumbent review and 4-6 weeks for review and selection. Dates are announced in Q2.
sections.plainLanguage: The person serves for a year and can be asked back. Anyone can suggest someone, even themselves, and the IAB then picks.

sections.title: Mid-term Vacancies and Other Notes
sections.content:
If the IETF-appointed member cannot serve a full term, the IAB may immediately select a replacement for the remainder using an interim process with a separately announced timeline. If it does not, the next annual process fills the vacancy.

The document requires no IANA actions and says it describes no technical protocols and has no implications for network security.
sections.plainLanguage: If the chosen person has to leave early, the IAB can quickly pick a stand-in or wait for the next yearly pick.
